facts.statement: Chilantaisaurus fossils date to the Late Cretaceous period, specifically younger than approximately 92 million years ago.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous, ?(younger than ~92 Ma)

facts.statement: The genus Chilantaisaurus was described by the Chinese paleontologist Hu Show-Yung in 1964.
facts.quote: It was described by Chinese paleontologist Hu Show-Yung in 1964.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Chilantaisaurus was discovered by a joint Sino-Soviet expedition in Inner Mongolia within the Ulansuhai Formation.
facts.quote: This specimen was found by a joint Sino-Soviet expedition to Inner Mongolia in rock layers coming from the Ulansuhai Formation.

facts.statement: The Ulansuhai Formation containing Chilantaisaurus fossils is estimated to date from the Santonian to Campanian stages, between 85.7 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: These rock layers are thought to date to the Santonian or Campanian stages of the Cretaceous period, around 85.7 to 72.2 million years ago.

facts.statement: The exact age of the Ulansuhai Formation is currently debated among researchers.
facts.quote: However, the age of the Ulansuhai Formation is debated.

facts.statement: Chilantaisaurus reached a length of approximately 11 meters and weighed between 2.5 and 4 metric tons.
facts.quote: Chilantaisaurus was around 11 m in length and weighed 2.5 - 4 MT.

facts.statement: The known forelimb bones of Chilantaisaurus include a humerus that is among the largest found in any theropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: The forelimbs of Chilantaisaurus are only known from a humerus and a manual ungual (hand claw); this humerus is one of the largest humeri known from a theropod dinosaur.

facts.statement: Chilantaisaurus possessed long hindlimbs with a robust metatarsus, which is the largest known among purported megaraptorans or Neovenator.
facts.quote: The hindlimbs were long with a robust metatarsus, the largest known of any purported megaraptoran or Neovenator itself.

facts.statement: Chilantaisaurus fossils were first discovered in 1960 at the Tashuikou site in Inner Mongolia, China, by a Sino-Soviet expedition.
facts.quote: Fossils assigned to Chilantaisaurus were first discovered in 1960 by members of a Sino-Soviet expedition at the Tashuikou site, 60 km north of Jilantai Salt Lake in the eastern Alashan Desert in Inner Mongolia, China.

facts.statement: The Chilantaisaurus remains found at Tashuikou consisted of fragmentary forelimb and hindlimb bones cataloged as IVPP V.2884.1 at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.
facts.quote: The remains of Chilantaisaurus found consisted of fragmentary forelimb and hindlimb bones likely from the same individual, and were cataloged as IVPP V.2884.1 at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Beijing.

facts.statement: In 1964, Hu Show-Yung formally described the Tashuikou fossils as the new species Chilantaisaurus tashuikouensis.
facts.quote: In 1964, Chinese paleontologist Hu Show-Yung scientifically described the remains and assigned them to a new genus and species of carnosaurian theropod, which they named Chilantaisaurus tashuikouensis.

facts.statement: The genus name Chilantaisaurus combines the local name Chilantai Salt Lake with the Greek word for lizard, sauros.
facts.quote: The generic name is a combination of Chilantai (in reference to the Salt Lake near where the fossils were found) and the Greek word sauros meaning "lizard", a common suffix for dinosaur names.

facts.statement: Although Hu did not designate a type specimen in 1964, later researchers selected the right humerus as the lectotype and the remaining material as paralectotypes.
facts.quote: Hu (1964) did not select a lectotype or holotype specimen, though Benson and Xing (2008) chose the right humerus as the lectotype and the rest of the material were designated as paralectotypes.

facts.statement: Several fossils originally assigned to C. tashuikouensis by Hu are now considered indeterminate because they do not overlap with the main type material.
facts.quote: In his description, Hu also assigned an isolated tooth, mid caudal vertebra, and distal (away from body) caudal vertebra to C. tashuikouensis; however none of these remains have overlap with the lectotype or paralectotypes and were not associated with those specimens, leaving their statuses in question.

facts.statement: The original describer Hu classified Chilantaisaurus as a carnosaur, but this classification has been challenged by later studies.
facts.quote: Hu believed it was a member of Carnosauria; later studies have challenged this notion.

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate regarding the classification of Chilantaisaurus, with proposals ranging from spinosaurid to coelurosaurian or carcharodontosaurian affinities.
facts.quote: While some studies suggested it was a member of Spinosauridae, others have proposed that Chilantaisaurus was a coelurosaur, possibly related to Megaraptora, or a carcharodontosaurian related to genera like Neovenator.

facts.statement: The environment where Chilantaisaurus lived was a floodplain characterized by meandering rivers, as indicated by the red mudstone and siltstone of the formation.
facts.quote: The Ulansuhai Formation is dominated by red mudstone and siltstone, indicating a floodplain environment defined by meandering rivers.

facts.statement: Hu named the species Chilantaisaurus maortuensis in the same 1964 paper where he described C. tashuikouensis.
facts.quote: Chilantaisaurus maortuensis was named by Hu in 1964 in the same paper describing C. tashuikouensis.

facts.statement: The species C. maortuensis has been reclassified multiple times, moving from Alashansaurus to Shaochilong, where it is classified as a carcharodontosaurid.
facts.quote: In 2000, American paleontologist Daniel Chure assigned it to its own genus, "Alashansaurus", in a thesis; however American researcher Steve Brusatte and colleagues (2009) placed it in the new genus Shaochilong, which they classified as a carcharodontosaurid.

facts.statement: The species C. zheziangensis was named in 1979 based on fossils found in the Upper Cretaceous Tangshang Formation in Zhejiang Province, China.
facts.quote: Chilantaisaurus zheziangensis was named by Chinese paleontologist Dong Zhiming in 1979 on the basis of an incomplete right tibia and complete pes that had been found in 1972 in an outcrop of the Upper Cretaceous-aged Tangshang Formation in Zhejiang Province, China.

facts.statement: Recent studies suggest that C. zheziangensis is likely an indeterminate therizinosaur rather than a species of Chilantaisaurus.
facts.quote: Dong believed it was a species of Chilantaisaurus based on perceived similarities in their unguals; however recent studies have concluded that it likely comes from an indeterminate therizinosaur.

facts.statement: Chilantaisaurus was a large theropod dinosaur that measured 11 meters in length and weighed between 2.5 and 4 metric tons.
facts.quote: Chilantaisaurus was a large theropod, measuring 11 m long and weighing 2.5 - 4 MT.

facts.statement: A crescent-shaped, pitted muscle scar on the anterior surface of the humeral deltopectoral crest is unique to Chilantaisaurus among theropods.
facts.quote: On the anterior surface of the crest is a crescent-shaped, pitted muscle scar that is unique to the species among theropods.

facts.statement: The known fragment of the ilium in Chilantaisaurus is extremely thin, measuring only 6 to 7 mm in transverse diameter.
facts.quote: The ilium fragment is extremely thin relative to its size, measuring a mere 6-7 mm in transverse diameter.

facts.statement: The metatarsus of Chilantaisaurus is 450 mm long and estimated to be 200 mm wide, which is larger than that of Neovenator or any known megaraptoran.
facts.quote: In total, the metatarsus is 450 mm in length and an estimated 200 mm in width, larger than in Neovenator or any megaraptoran known.

facts.statement: In 1964, the genus was originally classified by Hu as a member of Carnosauria related to Allosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1964, Hu regarded Chilantaisaurus as a member of Carnosauria somewhat related to Allosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2012, Allain and colleagues classified Chilantaisaurus within Spinosauridae based on traits such as a high humeral to femoral length ratio and an enlarged manual ungual.
facts.quote: In 2012, Allain and colleagues classified the genus in Spinosauridae because of its high humeral to femoral length ratio, straight humeral shaft in lateral view, enlarged manual ungual, and a robust longitudinal ridge near the astragalar facet, all traits similar to or found in spinosaurids.

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate regarding the classification of Chilantaisaurus, with some studies placing it in Spinosauridae while others have not.
facts.quote: Several studies have classified Chilantaisaurus as a spinosaurid or spinosauroid, although Chilantaisaurus has not been classified as a spinosaurid in many studies since.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Chilantaisaurus weighed about 6 metric tons; while some researchers estimate this based on femur length comparisons to Tyrannosaurus, others argue that femoral circumference relates to locomotor load capacity rather than body mass.
facts.quote: While Brusatte and colleagues (2010) estimated that Chilantaisaurus might have weighed about 6 MT based on femur length similar to that of Tyrannosaurus, Persons and colleagues (2020) argued that greater femoral circumference indicates a greater capacity to withstand greater locomotor loads, not greater body mass.

facts.statement: If Chilantaisaurus is confirmed as a spinosaurid, it would represent one of the few spinosaurids found in Asia and potentially the youngest member of the clade.
facts.quote: If Chilantaisaurus were a spinosaurid, it would be the youngest member of the clade and one of the few spinosaurids unearthed in Asia.

facts.statement: A 2010 study by Benson, Carrano, and Brusatte classified Chilantaisaurus as a member of the clade Neovenatoridae within Megaraptora.
facts.quote: In a 2010 study, American paleontologists Roger Benson, Matthew Carrano, and Steve Brusatte found Chilantaisaurus to be a member of a monophyletic clade named Neovenatoridae, along with the group Megaraptora.

facts.statement: Several authors have proposed an earlier origin for the clade Neovenatoridae than suggested by Benson and colleagues.
facts.quote: However several authors proposed an earlier origin for Neovenatoridae.

facts.statement: A 2019 redescription by Aranciaga Rolando, Novas, and Agnolín placed Megaraptora, including Chilantaisaurus, in a polytomy at the base of Tyrannosauroidea.
facts.quote: A 2019 redescription of Murusraptor by Argentine paleontologists Alexis Aranciaga Rolando, Novas and Federico Agnolín continued to find Megaraptora in a polytomy at the base of Tyrannosauroidea, based on the dataset of Apesteguía and colleagues (2016).

facts.statement: A 2018 analysis by Porfiri and colleagues suggested Chilantaisaurus is a basal coelurosaur of unknown affinities, placing it in a polytomy with Gualicho, Megaraptora, and Tyrannoraptora.
facts.quote: A phylogenetic analysis by Argentine paleontologist Juan D. Porfiri and colleagues (2018) supported this idea and Chilantaisaurus was found in polytomy with Gualicho, Megaraptora, and Tyrannoraptora, suggesting that the taxon is a basal coelurosaur of unknown affinities.

facts.statement: The fossil range of Chilantaisaurus is the Upper Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cretácico Superior

facts.statement: Chilantaisaurus was a large theropod measuring 11 to 13 meters in length and weighing an estimated 2.5 to 4 metric tons.
facts.quote: Chilantaisaurus era un gran terópodo, tenía 11 metros a 13 metros de largo con un peso estimado de entre 2.5 toneladas y 4 toneladas métricas.

facts.statement: In 2010, Brusatte et al. estimated the weight of Chilantaisaurus at 6 tons based on femur length measurements.
facts.quote: En 2010, Brusatte et al. estimó que pesaba 6 toneladas, según las mediciones de longitud del fémur.

facts.statement: Only a partial skull and a few vertebrae of Chilantaisaurus have been found.

facts.statement: Chilantaisaurus possessed a short axis with straight neural spines.

facts.statement: The Ulansuhai Formation, where Chilantaisaurus fossils were found, indicates a floodplain environment defined by meandering rivers.
facts.quote: The Ulansuhai Formation is dominated by red mudstone and siltstone, indicating a floodplain environment defined by meandering rivers.

facts.statement: Geologic features like calcrete in the Ulansuhai Formation indicate drier components of the ecosystem where Chilantaisaurus lived.

facts.statement: The Ulansuhai Formation was deposited during a transition period in the Gobi from wet, fluvial ecosystems to desertic, dune-dominated ecosystems.
